lessons.title: Label the circuit
lessons.intro: Before anyone powers a board, it needs a label: its name and its supply voltage.
lessons.doneSub: Name, voltage and a clean label line, ready for the bench.

questions.ask: What does Python print?
questions.hint: Look at which name has quote marks around it.
questions.ok: name without quotes is the stored text; "name" in quotes is the word itself. Python prints text without its quote marks.

fb.b: Python leaves out the quote marks when it prints text.
fb.c: In quotes, "name" is a word, not the variable.

questions.bridge: store the board's supply voltage.
questions.label: Circuit A: a battery, one resistor and an ammeter.

science.title: Why label a circuit?
science.text: Labs share benches and boards. A name and supply voltage on every board stops someone connecting 12 V to a board built for 5 V.

codeNote.title: Text and names
codeNote.text: Quote marks make text. A name without them refers to a stored value.

questions.ask: Store the supply voltage as a number
questions.hint: Think about what * would do to each option.
questions.ok: 12 is a number, so volts * 2 is 24. In quotes, "12" is text, and text times 2 repeats it: 1212.

fb.b: "12" is text, and text times 2 repeats it: 1212.
fb.c: twelve is not defined, so Python stops with a NameError.
fb.d: 12V is not valid Python; it stops with a SyntaxError.

questions.bridge: make one label from the name and the voltage.
questions.label: The battery of Circuit A, with its voltage still to be stored.

science.title: Why voltage is a number
science.text: Every later calculation, current, power, safe limits, needs the voltage as a number. Stored as text, the maths silently goes wrong.

codeNote.title: Numbers and text
codeNote.text: Python stores numbers and text as different types, and each type behaves differently.

questions.ask: What does the label line print?
questions.hint: Look at where the spaces sit.
questions.ok: str(volts) turns 12 into "12", and + joins the pieces with their spaces: Circuit A at 12 V.

fb.b: Without quotes, volts means its value, 12.
fb.c: The spaces are inside the quoted pieces, so they stay.

questions.bridge: the technician's script stops with an error.
questions.label: A label tag waiting to be written for Circuit A.

science.title: Labels that read like a sentence
science.text: A label such as "Circuit A at 12 V" can be read at a glance on a crowded bench, which is what safety labels are for.

codeNote.title: Joining text
codeNote.text: `+` can join pieces of text into one.

questions.ask: The technician's script stops. Which line?
questions.hint: Look for a line that mixes two different types.
questions.ok: volts is a number, and + cannot join text to a number, so Python stops. str(volts) fixes it.

fb.b: Storing the voltage as a number is right.
fb.d: print() is fine; Python never reaches it.

questions.bridge: write the label for the panel.
questions.label: The technician's script stops with a TypeError.

science.title: Why scripts should fail loudly
science.text: A script that stops with a clear error is safer than one that prints a wrong label onto a live board.

codeNote.title: Types in one line
codeNote.text: Every value has a type, such as text or a number. Some operations need both sides to match.

pics.text: My label script stops. Python says: can only concatenate str (not "int") to str.

questions.after: After the fix: Circuit A at 12 V

questions.ask: Write the panel label in one line
questions.hint: One letter in front of the quotes changes what the braces do.
questions.ok: An f-string fills each {name} with its value, so no str() is needed: Circuit A: 12 V.

fb.b: r means raw text, so the braces print as they are: {name}: {volts} V.
fb.c: b makes bytes, so Python prints b'{name}: {volts} V'.

questions.bridge: see your finished label.
questions.label: The control panel label for Circuit A.

science.title: Panel labels
science.text: Control panels carry short, standard labels so an engineer can check every circuit's supply without opening the case.

codeNote.title: String prefixes
codeNote.text: A letter placed before a quote mark changes how Python reads that text.

lessons.title: Ohm's law
lessons.intro: Our 12 V supply drives a 4 Ω resistor. Can you check the current and power before we switch on?
lessons.doneSub: The current, the power and a safe rating, all from one script.

questions.ask: What current does Python print?
questions.hint: Think about whether Python keeps decimals when it divides.
questions.ok: I = V / R = 12 / 4. Python's / always gives a decimal number, a float, so it prints 3.0. // would give 3.

fb.b: / always gives a float in Python; 12 // 4 would give 3.
fb.c: That multiplies instead of dividing.

questions.bridge: work out the power.
questions.label: A 12 volt battery driving a 4 ohm resistor; the current is unknown.

science.title: Ohm's law
science.text: The current through a resistor is the voltage across it divided by its resistance: I = V / R. It is the first check before powering anything.

codeNote.title: Division
codeNote.text: Python has more than one division operator, and they give different kinds of number.

questions.ask: Work out the power
questions.hint: Which operation turns volts and amps into watts?
questions.ok: P = V × I = 12 × 3.0 = 36.0 W. ** would raise 12 to a power instead.

fb.b: 12 / 3.0 is 4.0, the resistance again.
fb.c: ** is a power in the maths sense: 12 ** 3.0 is 1728.0.
fb.d: 12 + 3.0 is 15.0; power multiplies.

questions.bridge: add a second resistor in series.
questions.label: The same circuit; the power it uses is the blank.

science.title: Electrical power
science.text: Power, P = V × I, is how fast a part turns electrical energy into heat or work. Resistors and supplies have a maximum power they can handle.

codeNote.title: Arithmetic operators
codeNote.text: Python uses symbols such as `+`, `-`, `*`, `/` and `**` for maths.

questions.ask: Add 3 Ω in series. What is the current now?
questions.hint: Combine the two resistors first.
questions.ok: 4 Ω + 3 Ω in series is 7 Ω, so I = 12 / 7 = 1.714..., and round(I, 2) gives 1.71.

fb.b: That is before rounding.
fb.c: That was the current with 4 Ω alone.

questions.bridge: your partner's power reading looks too high.
questions.label: Two resistors in series, 4 and 3 ohms; the new current is unknown.

science.title: Resistors in series
science.text: Resistors in a line add up: 4 Ω and 3 Ω behave like one 7 Ω resistor, so the same voltage pushes less current.

codeNote.title: Rounding
codeNote.text: `round()` controls how many decimal places you see.

questions.ask: Partner's script says 39 W. Which line?
questions.hint: Look at which numbers each operation applies to.
questions.ok: Python works out V ** 2 / 4 first, then adds 3: 36 + 3 = 39.0. It should divide by R_total.

fb.b: The series resistance is 7 Ω.
fb.d: print() shows what P holds.

questions.bridge: check the power against the resistor's rating.
questions.label: Your lab partner's script says the power is 39 watts.

science.title: Checking before buying parts
science.text: A wrong power figure leads to buying oversized parts, or worse, undersized ones that overheat. Recheck the formula before changing the design.

codeNote.title: Order of operations
codeNote.text: Python follows maths order when a line has several operations.

pics.text: My script says 39 W, and the resistor is only rated 25 W. Do we need a bigger one?

questions.ask: Is the power under the 25 W rating?
questions.hint: Compare the power with the rating.
questions.ok: P is 144 / 7, about 20.6 W, so P < 25 is True: the resistor stays within its rating.
questions.bridge: see your finished circuit check.
questions.label: A resistor rated 25 watts; whether it is safe is unknown.

science.title: Power ratings
science.text: Every resistor has a power rating. Running it above that rating overheats it, so engineers keep a safety margin below the limit.

codeNote.title: Comparisons
codeNote.text: Symbols such as `<` and `>` compare two values.

questions.wrongBuild: The line is safe = P < 25: a comparison gives True or False, stored in safe.

lessons.title: Sort the fruit
lessons.intro: The colour sensor reads how much of each fruit is covered in dark spots. Over 30% is spoilt, and the pusher sends it to the bin.
lessons.doneSub: Spoilt fruit goes to the bin, the rest stays on the belt.

questions.ask: The sensor reads 45%. What happens?
questions.hint: Compare the reading with the limit in the code.
questions.ok: 45 > 30 is True, so the pusher bins the spotted orange. The clean apple has no instruction yet, so it rolls off the end.

fb.b: The condition is True here, so the indented line runs.
fb.c: if uses True or False to decide; it does not print it.

questions.bridge: decide what happens to good fruit.
questions.label: A spotted orange under the colour sensor, with a clean apple behind it. Only the spoilt case has a rule so far.

science.title: Sensors and actuators
science.text: A sorting line pairs a sensor, here a colour camera, with an actuator, the pusher. The code in between decides.

codeNote.title: Decisions with `if`
codeNote.text: `if` checks a condition. The indented lines below it belong to it.

questions.ask: Good fruit should stay on the belt
questions.hint: What should the line do when the check fails?
questions.ok: else runs whenever the if check is False: 12 > 30 is False, so the pear stays on the belt. Now every fruit has a place to go.

fb.b: elif needs a condition after it; on its own Python stops with a SyntaxError.
fb.c: if needs a condition; if: on its own is a SyntaxError.
fb.d: Python has no "else if"; it is a SyntaxError. The word is elif.

questions.bridge: add a third path for nearly-ripe fruit.
questions.label: A clean pear under the sensor, 12% spots, with a spoilt strawberry behind it.

science.title: Every item needs a route
science.text: On a production line, every item has to end up somewhere planned. An item with no route is a jam or a loss.

codeNote.title: Another path
codeNote.text: An `if` can be followed by a block that runs in the other case.

questions.ask: The sensor reads 20%. Where does it go?
questions.hint: Python reads the checks from the top.
questions.ok: 20 > 30 is False, then 20 > 15 is True, so the peach goes to the juice line and Python skips the rest.

fb.b: Only fruit over 30% goes to the bin.
fb.c: else only runs when every condition above it is False.

questions.bridge: your mentor's pusher is binning good fruit.
questions.label: Three fruits: a lightly marked peach, a clean apple and a spoilt lemon, with three places to go.

science.title: Grading, not only sorting
science.text: Real lines grade produce: perfect fruit for shops, marked fruit for juice, spoilt fruit to waste.

codeNote.title: More than two paths
codeNote.text: A decision can have several checks in a row.

questions.ask: The pusher bins good fruit. Which line?
questions.hint: Read the condition aloud and compare it with the rule.
questions.ok: < 30 is True for clean fruit, so the pusher fired on good fruit. Spoilt means more than 30: spots > 30.

fb.c: The message is right; it runs for the wrong fruit.

questions.bridge: catch soft fruit as well.
questions.label: The sorter as your mentor sees it: clean fruit keeps being pushed into the bin.

science.title: Failing the wrong way
science.text: A flipped threshold makes a machine do the opposite of its job at full speed. Engineers test each branch with known items.

codeNote.title: Comparison direction
codeNote.text: `>` and `<` point in opposite directions.

questions.after: After the fix: nothing prints for 12%

questions.ask: Bin fruit that is spotted or soft
questions.hint: Re-read the question: does the fruit need both problems?

questions.label: A pear with few spots that the firmness sensor reads as soft.

science.title: Two sensors, one decision
science.text: Spots show on the surface, but rot can start inside. A second sensor for firmness catches fruit the camera misses.

codeNote.title: Combining checks
codeNote.text: Python can join two conditions into one with a word between them.

lessons.title: Dose by weight
lessons.intro: Training example: Drug X is dosed at 10 mg per kg of body weight, up to 500 mg. Check each dose in code before it reaches the ward.
lessons.doneSub: The right dose, capped at the maximum, and the volume to draw up.

questions.ask: What dose does Python print?
questions.hint: Read the dose rule in the goal screen again.
questions.ok: 42 kg × 10 mg per kg = 420 mg.

fb.b: That adds 10 instead of multiplying.
fb.c: That divides by 10 instead of multiplying.

questions.bridge: read a weight typed into a form.
questions.label: A 42 kg patient and an empty syringe; the dose is unknown until you answer.

science.title: Weight-based dosing
science.text: Many medicines, especially for children, are dosed per kilogram, so the same drug gives different doses to different patients.

codeNote.title: Variables
codeNote.text: A name such as `weight` stores a value you can use in later lines.

questions.ask: The weight arrives from a form as text
questions.hint: The form gives you text. What does the maths need?
questions.ok: int() turns the text "42" into the number 42, so the maths works: 420. Without it, "42" * 10 repeats the text ten times.

fb.b: str() keeps it as text, and text times 10 repeats it: 42424242424242424242.
fb.c: len() gives the number of characters, 2, so it prints 20.
fb.d: print() shows the text and returns None, and None * 10 stops with a TypeError.

questions.bridge: cap the dose for a heavier patient.
questions.label: A form field holding the weight as text, "42".

science.title: Data from forms
science.text: Electronic prescribing systems read weights from typed forms. Converting and checking every input is a basic safety step.

codeNote.title: Types of value
codeNote.text: Text and numbers are different types. Python can convert between them.

kw.label: A syringe that fills to the dose once the weight is a number

questions.ask: A 63 kg patient. What dose does Python print?
questions.hint: Look at what min() is given.
questions.ok: 63 × 10 is 630, but min() keeps the smaller of 630 and 500, so the dose stops at the 500 mg maximum.

fb.b: That is before the maximum is applied.
fb.c: min() compares the two values; it does not add them.

questions.bridge: the pharmacist's script gives everyone 500 mg.
questions.entry: Dose for 63 kg: capped at 500 mg
questions.label: A 63 kg patient; the syringe has a maximum line at 500 mg.

science.title: Maximum doses
science.text: Weight-based doses usually have a ceiling, so a heavy patient never receives more than the safe maximum.

codeNote.title: Smaller of two
codeNote.text: `min()` gives back the smallest of the values you pass it.

kw.label: A syringe with a 500 mg maximum line

questions.ask: Everyone gets 500 mg. Which line is wrong?
questions.hint: Compare what this line does with the dose rule.
questions.ok: max() keeps the larger value, so every patient gets at least 500 mg. min() caps the dose instead: 420 mg here.

fb.c: print() shows what dose holds.

questions.bridge: work out the volume to draw up.
questions.label: Before Check the syringe keeps filling to 500 mg for a 42 kg patient, which is too much.

science.title: Why dose errors matter
science.text: Dosing errors are one of the most common medication errors in hospitals, which is why pharmacists double-check calculations.

codeNote.title: Functions with similar names
codeNote.text: Some built-in functions come in pairs that do opposite jobs.

kw.label: The syringe filling past the right dose

questions.label: A 10 mL syringe; the volume to draw up is unknown.

science.title: From dose to volume
science.text: Nurses give medicine by volume, so the dose in mg is turned into mL using the stock strength printed on the vial.

codeNote.title: Building an expression
codeNote.text: An expression combines names, numbers and operators into one value.

lessons.title: Early warning alert
lessons.intro: NEWS2 scores each vital sign. For pulse: 51 to 90 scores 0, 91 to 110 scores 1, 111 to 130 scores 2, 131 or more scores 3.
lessons.doneSub: Pulse bands scored in the right order, and the doctor alerted when it matters.

questions.ask: The pulse is 135. What prints?
questions.hint: Compare the reading with the band in the code.
questions.ok: 135 >= 131 is True, so the indented line runs: a pulse that high scores 3 in NEWS2.

fb.b: The condition is True here, so the indented line runs.
fb.c: if uses True or False to decide; it does not print it.

questions.bridge: score the pulse with two bands.
questions.label: A bedside monitor showing a pulse of 135.

science.title: What NEWS2 is
science.text: NEWS2 is the National Early Warning Score used across NHS hospitals. Each vital sign earns points, and higher totals call for faster review.

codeNote.title: Decisions with `if`
codeNote.text: `if` checks a condition. The indented lines below it belong to it.

args: A bedside monitor showing a pulse of 135 beats per minute

questions.hint: The second band should only be checked when the first one fails.
questions.ok: elif is only checked when the if above it is False. 135 >= 131 is True, so score stays 3. A second if would also run and overwrite it with 2.

fb.c: else takes no condition; with pulse >= 111 after it, Python stops with a SyntaxError.
fb.d: or cannot start a line; Python stops with a SyntaxError.

questions.bridge: add every pulse band.
questions.label: The monitor still shows 135; which band applies is the blank.

science.title: Bands, not single cut-offs
science.text: NEWS2 splits each vital sign into bands, so the score grows with how far a reading is from normal.

science.title: Small scores add up
science.text: A score of 1 on its own is low, but NEWS2 adds the scores of all vital signs, so several small changes can still raise the alarm.

codeNote.title: A chain of checks
codeNote.text: A decision can have several checks in a row, ending with a fallback.

science.text: A score that comes out too low is dangerous because nothing looks wrong. Testing each band with a known reading catches it.

codeNote.text: In a chain of checks, the order decides which one wins.

lessons.title: Battery life
lessons.intro: Our robot runs on a 2000 mAh battery and draws 300 mA. How long will it last between charges?
